summary: Defines requirements for protocols used by Network Access Servers, the devices that let users connect to a network.

plainLanguage.summary: A network access server is the box that gives a user a connection. This memo is a checklist for the protocol that server uses to check who the user is, decide what they may do and record what they used. It is written as requirements to be measured against, not as a protocol to implement.

questions: what is a network access server
what attributes must an aaa protocol support
subtitle: A checklist of what an authentication, authorization and accounting protocol must do for network access servers.

tldr.problem: Network access servers, the devices that give a user a connection, need a protocol for checking who the user is, deciding what they may do and recording what they used, and the existing choices do not all cover what a real deployment needs.
tldr.mechanism: The memo divides the protocols around a NAS into four spaces, access, network, AAA and device management, and then lists requirements for each, with most of the detail on AAA: transport independence, load balancing and failover, an attribute-value model, mutual authentication, and what authentication, authorization and accounting data must carry.
tldr.outcome: It is a criteria document rather than a protocol. The requirements are written as MUST and SHOULD so that a candidate protocol can be measured against them. The memo is Informational.

facts.label: Protocol spaces around a NAS
facts.value: 4: access, network, AAA and device management

facts.label: Minimum attribute space
facts.value: 64K attributes of 16 bits, each at least 64K long

facts.label: Real time accounting
facts.value: Delivery beginning within one second of the triggering event

facts.label: Expiry types that must be supported
facts.value: Total session time, idle time, bytes transmitted and bytes received

facts.label: Access protocol baseline
facts.value: PPP, except for legacy text logins such as telnet, rlogin or LAT

today: RFC 3169 is an Informational memo listing the requirements that an AAA protocol used by network access servers must meet, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. Its security section points back to the requirements in the document itself, and its IANA section asks that new attributes and values be registrable directly through IANA rather than through a full standardization process. The NAS model it builds on is in RFC 2881.

sections.title: The Four Spaces of NAS Protocols
sections.content:
The memo defines requirements for protocols used by Network Access Servers. The protocols used by a NAS may be divided into four spaces: access protocols, network protocols, AAA protocols and device management protocols. The primary focus of the document is on AAA protocols, which cover authentication, authorization and accounting. The reference model of a NAS used by the document, and the analysis of the functions of a NAS that led to these requirements, are in the NAS Model document.

The requirements language is the usual one: the key words MAY, MUST, MUST NOT, optional, recommended, SHOULD and SHOULD NOT are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: Four kinds of protocol surround a network access server. The memo is mainly about the third one, the AAA protocol, which covers checking identity, deciding access and recording usage.

sections.title: Access and Network Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
There are three basic types of access protocol used by a NAS. First are the traditional telephony-based access protocols, which interface to the NAS via a modem or terminal adapter or similar device, and which typically support asynchronous or synchronous PPP carried over a telephony protocol. Second are broadband pseudo-telephony access protocols, carried over xDSL or cable modems, which typically support an encapsulation method such as PPP over Ethernet. Finally are the virtual access protocols used by NASs that terminate tunnels, one example of this type being L2TP.

It is a central assumption of the NAS model used here that a NAS accepts multiple point-to-point links via one of the above access protocols. So at a minimum, any NAS access protocol MUST be able to carry PPP. The exception to this requirement is for NASs that support legacy text login methods such as telnet, rlogin or LAT; only these access protocols are exempt from the requirement to support PPP.

The network protocols supported by a NAS depend entirely on the kind of network to which the NAS is providing access, and the document imposes no additional requirements beyond the protocol specifications themselves. For example, a NAS that serves a routed network and includes internet routing functionality must adhere to the requirements for IP version 4 routers, but there are no additional protocol requirements imposed by virtue of the device being a NAS.
sections.plainLanguage: Whatever the user's line looks like, the access protocol has to be able to carry PPP, because that is what the rest of the system expects. Only the old text-login style of access, such as telnet, is let off that hook.

sections.title: General AAA Protocol Characteristics
sections.content:
Certain general characteristics apply to any AAA protocol used by NASs, and the transport requirements for authentication and authorization need not be the same as those for accounting and auditing. An AAA protocol suite MAY use the same transport and protocol for both functions, but this is not strictly required.

The design MUST be transport independent, because existing infrastructures use UDP-based protocols such as RADIUS and gateways to new protocols must be practical to encourage migration. It MUST comply with the congestion control recommendations in RFC 2914.

Very large scale NASs serving up to thousands of simultaneous sessions are now being deployed, and a single server system may service a large number of ports, so in the extreme there may be an almost constant exchange of many small packets between the NASs and the AAA server. The transport SHOULD therefore support being optimized for a long-term exchange of small packets in a stream between a pair of hosts. The protocol MUST be designed to support a large number of ports, clients and concurrent sessions. Examples of poor design are given: message identifiers whose values are so small that queues and reception windows wrap under load, unique session identifier ranges so small that they wrap within the lifetime of potential long sessions, counter values that cannot accommodate reasonable current and future bandwidth usage, and computational processes with high overhead that must be performed frequently.

To support large loads, load balancing and fail-over to multiple AAA servers will be required. The protocol MUST provide for NASs to balance individual AAA requests between two or more AAA servers, and the load balancing mechanism SHOULD be built into the protocol itself. It MUST be able to detect a failure of the transport to deliver a message or messages within a known and controllable time period, so it can engage retransmission or server fail-over processes, and the reliability and robustness of authentication requests MUST be predictable and configurable. The design MUST NOT introduce a single point of failure during the AAA process, and MUST allow sessions between a NAS and a given AAA server to fail over to a secondary server without loss of state information.

NASs operated by one authority may provide network access services for clients operated by another authority, to network destinations operated by yet another authority, and the memo notes that this arrangement is of growing importance, with dial roaming now a nearly ubiquitous service. The protocol MUST support AAA services that travel between multiple domains of authority and MUST NOT use a model that assumes a single domain of authority. It MUST NOT dictate particular business models for the relationship between the administrative domains, and it MUST support proxy, and SHOULD support other multi-domain relationships such as brokering and referral.

The protocol SHOULD use an Attribute-Value representation for AAA data, since years of operational experience have proven that model to be an optimal representation, though even if the on-the-wire representation is different, Attribute-Value can serve as an abstraction for discussing AAA information. The protocol MUST support a minimum of 64K attributes of 16 bits each, each with a minimum length of 64K of 16 bits, because attribute space tends to run out quickly. It MUST support simple attribute data types including integer, enumeration, text string, IP address and date and time, and MUST provide some support for complex structured data types. Wherever IP addresses are carried it MUST support both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, and wherever text information is carried it MUST comply with the IETF policy on character sets and languages.

At a minimum the protocol MUST support, or be easily extended to support, the set of attributes supported by RADIUS and RADIUS Accounting; if the base protocol does not support the complete set, an extension to that protocol MUST be defined which does. It MUST provide a built-in extensibility mechanism, which MUST include a means for adding new standard attribute extensions and a method for registering or requesting extensions through IANA, so that long-term working group involvement is not required to create new attribute types, and it SHOULD separate the specification of the transport from the specification of the attributes. It MUST include a means for individual vendors to add value through vendor-specific attributes and SHOULD support vendor-specific data types.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol must not be tied to one way of carrying messages, must cope with thousands of sessions at once, must spread the load over several AAA servers and survive one of them failing, and must not assume that the operator, the user and the destination all belong to the same organisation.

sections.title: Authentication and User Security Requirements
sections.content:
The AAA protocol MUST provide mutual authentication between the AAA server and the NAS, because it is poor security practice for a NAS to communicate with an AAA server that is not trusted and vice versa. At a minimum the protocol SHOULD support a secret shared pairwise between each NAS and AAA server to mutually verify identity, which is intended for small-scale deployments, and it MAY provide stronger mutual security techniques. Because shared secrets are difficult to deploy properly at large scale and it is tempting for operators to use a single shared secret, which rarely changes, across all NASs, the protocol MUST also support mutual verification of identity using a public key infrastructure that supports expiration and revocation of keys. And because some attributes are more operationally sensitive than others, and in a multi-domain scenario attributes may be inserted by servers from different administrative domains, the protocol MUST support selective encryption of attributes on an attribute-by-attribute basis, even within the same message, for authentication, authorization and accounting data alike.

End users requesting network access present various types of credentials, and it is the purpose of the AAA protocol to transport these credentials between the NAS and the AAA server. The protocol MUST support transport of credentials from the AAA server to the NAS, between the user and the NAS, and between the NAS and the AAA server. It MUST support re-authentication at any time during a session, initiated from either side, which is a requirement of CHAP. It MUST be able to support multi-phase authentication methods, including text prompting from the NAS to the user, a series of binary challenges and responses of arbitrary length, an authentication failure reason transmitted from the NAS to the user, and callback to a pre-determined phone number. Because security protocol development is constant and today's secure methods may be proven insecure tomorrow, the protocol MUST provide some support for adding new authentication credential types.

Beyond the minimum attribute set, the protocol must support and define attributes providing further functions. It MUST be able to act as an intermediary protocol between the authenticator and the authenticatee for PPP Password Authentication, PPP Challenge Handshake and PPP Extensible Authentication. It MUST be able to carry a user name in the form of a Network Access Identifier, an EAP Identity Request Type packet, and telephony dialling information such as Dialed Number Identification Service and Caller ID. If a particular type of credential is not needed for a session, the protocol MUST NOT require that dummy credentials be filled in: it MUST support authorization by identification or assertion only. It MUST also be able to carry, at a minimum, a secret or password, a response to a challenge presented by the NAS to the user, a one-time password, an X.509 digital certificate, and a Kerberos v5 ticket.

Where passwords are used as authentication credentials, the protocol MUST provide a secure means of hiding the password from intermediates in the AAA conversation, and where challenge and response mechanisms are used it MUST also prevent against replay attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The server and the access server must each be able to check the other's identity, and the protocol must be able to carry every kind of credential a user might have, from a password to a smart card certificate. Passwords must not be exposed to anything in between.

sections.title: Access Profiles and Resource Management
sections.content:
In all cases the protocol MUST specify that authorization data sent from the NAS to the AAA server is to be regarded as information or hints, and not directives. The protocol MUST be designed so that the AAA server makes all final authorization decisions and does not depend on a certain state being expected by the NAS.

The protocol MUST support dynamic re-authorization at any time during a user session, initiated in either direction, and that capability MUST include the ability to request a NAS to disconnect a user on demand. Resource management MUST be supported on demand by the NAS or the AAA server at any time during a session, meaning the ability for the NAS to allocate and deallocate shared resources from an AAA server servicing multiple NASes. Those resources may include IP addresses, concurrent usage limits, port usage limits and tunnel limits. The capability should have error detection and synchronization features that recover state after network and system failures, which may be accomplished by session information timeouts and explicit interim status and disconnect messages, and there should not be any dependencies on the Accounting message stream, as per current practices. This feature is primarily intended for NAS-local network resources; in a proxy or multi-domain environment, resource information should only be retained by the server doing the allocation and perhaps its backups, and authorization resources in remote domains should use the dynamic authorization features to change and revoke authorization status.

Because the AAA protocol is a primary means of gathering data used for making policy decisions, it MUST allow network operators to make policy decisions based on time and day restrictions, providing an unambiguous timestamp, NAS time zone indication and date indication; on location restrictions, providing an unambiguous location code that reflects the geographic location of the NAS, which is not the same type of thing as the dialling or dialled station; on dialling restrictions, providing accurate dialled and dialling station indications; and on concurrent login limitations, allowing the AAA server to limit concurrent logins by a particular user or group of users. The last mechanism need not be built into the protocol, but the protocol must provide sufficient authorization information for the AAA server to make that determination through an out-of-band mechanism.

When access is granted, a particular access profile is applied to the user's session, and the protocol MUST provide at least a means of applying profiles containing the following. IP address assignment, meaning a means of assigning an IPv4 or IPv6 address to an incoming user. Protocol filter application, by two different methods: selecting a protocol filter by reference to an identifier with the details of the filter action specified out of band, and passing a protocol filter by value, that is explicit passing of pass and block information by address range, TCP and UDP port number, and IP protocol number at a minimum. Compulsory tunnelling, meaning a means of directing a NAS to build a tunnel or tunnels to a specified endpoint, supporting creation of multiple simultaneous tunnels in a specified order, and specifying at a minimum the tunnel endpoints, tunnelling protocol type, underlying tunnel media type and tunnel authentication credentials; it MUST support at least the creation of tunnels using L2TP, ESP and AH, and MUST provide means of adding new tunnel types as they are standardized. Routing, meaning a means of assigning a particular static route to an incoming user session. Expirations and timeouts, of which total session time, idle time, total bytes transmitted and total bytes received MUST be supported. And quality of service parameters for the individual session.

The protocol MUST also provide a means of collecting resource state information and controlling resource allocation for network bandwidth usage per session, including multilink sessions, access port usage including concurrent usage and usage pools, connect time, IP addresses and pools, and compulsory tunnel limits. Where credentials used to authenticate compulsory tunnels are passed, the protocol MUST provide a means of securing them from end to end of the AAA conversation and MUST also provide protection against replay attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The access server only makes suggestions; the AAA server decides. What it decides includes the address, the filters, the tunnel, the route, the time limits and the service quality for the session, and it can change any of that while the user is online.

sections.title: Accounting and Auditing Requirements
sections.content:
The accounting and auditing functions of the AAA protocol are used for network planning, resource management, policy decisions and other functions that require accurate knowledge of the state of the NAS, so operators need to be able to engineer their network usage measurement systems to a predictable level of accuracy. The protocol MUST provide a means of guaranteed delivery of accounting information between the NAS and the AAA servers.

Operators often require a real time view onto the status of sessions served by a NAS, so the protocol MUST support real-time delivery of accounting and auditing information, and the memo defines real time as accounting information delivery beginning within one second of the triggering event. It SHOULD also support delivery of stored accounting and auditing information in batches. Because there may be delays associated with delivery, the protocol MUST carry an unambiguous time stamp associated with each accounting event, unambiguous with regard to time zone, which assumes the NAS has access to a reliable time source.

Delivery of accounting information MUST be supported when triggered by the following events: the start of a user session, the end of a user session, the expiration of a predetermined repeating time interval during a user session, for which the AAA server MUST be able to request that a NAS use a certain interval accounting time, dynamic re-authorization during a user session, and dynamic re-authentication during a user session. The protocol MUST also support a means of requesting current session state and accounting from the NAS on demand, so that operators maintain an accurate view even through the failure of an AAA server.

The accounting data itself MUST at a minimum cover all parameters used to authenticate a session, the details of the authorization profile that was applied to the session, the duration of the session, the cumulative number of bytes sent by the user during the session, the cumulative number of bytes received, the cumulative number of packets sent and received, and the details of the access protocol used during the session such as port type and connect speeds. Accounting and auditing data are operationally sensitive information, so the protocol MUST provide a means to assure end-to-end integrity of this data and SHOULD provide a means to assure the end-to-end confidentiality of it. Operators use accounting data for network planning, resource management and other business-critical functions that require confidence in the correctness of the data, so the protocol SHOULD provide a mechanism to ensure that the source of the data cannot easily repudiate it after transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: The record of what happened has to be reliable enough to plan a network and bill for it, so it must arrive, it must say when the event really happened rather than when the message was received, and the operator must be able to ask for the current state at any time.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PROTOCOL SPACES AROUND A NAS

items.title: Access protocols
items.text: How the user's line reaches the server: modems, broadband, and tunnel termination.

items.title: Network protocols
items.text: The routing and addressing the server provides over the network it serves.

items.title: AAA protocols
items.text: Checking who the user is, deciding what they may do, and recording what they used.

items.title: Device management protocols
items.text: How the server itself is configured and supervised.

viz.caption: THE CREDENTIAL TYPES THE PROTOCOL MUST CARRY

cells: The user's answer to a challenge presented by the NAS
A password that is used once
A certificate held by the user
A ticket issued by a Kerberos service

viz.caption: WHAT THE ACCESS PROFILE MUST BE ABLE TO CARRY

cells: An IPv4 or IPv6 address for the incoming user
A filter chosen by identifier, or passed by value with address ranges, port numbers and IP protocol numbers
The tunnel endpoints, tunnelling protocol type, media type and credentials, with support for L2TP, ESP and AH
A static route assigned to the session
Total session time, idle time, total bytes transmitted and total bytes received
Quality of Service parameters for the session
